questions.q: Why can a Public Read/Write OWD outperform a Private OWD on the same object at large data volumes?
options: Public Read/Write requires no sharing rows at all, since nothing beyond the default needs representing
Public Read/Write disables the role hierarchy entirely
Public Read/Write records are stored in a separate, faster database table
Private OWD always disables indexing on the object
questions.explain: When OWD is already the most open setting, no grant beyond the owner needs a sharing row, so there's nothing extra to store, index, or recalculate.

questions.q: What does the Row Cause field on a sharing row record?
options: The record's owner
The object's OWD setting
Why that particular grant exists (role, sharing rule, team, manual share, Apex reason)
The date the record was created
questions.explain: Row Cause explains the origin of a specific sharing grant, which is why querying a Share object by Row Cause is a fast way to debug access questions.

questions.q: A single queue owns 70,000 Cases under a Private OWD, several levels down a deep role hierarchy. What is the main architectural risk this creates?
options: The Cases become permanently inaccessible to everyone
Case escalation rules stop firing
The queue's Cases will be automatically moved to a Big Object
A role change above that queue could trigger a sharing recalculation large enough to lock up the org for hours
questions.explain: This is ownership skew: a large concentration of records under one owner, positioned under a hierarchy, means an upstream change can force recalculation across the whole skewed set at once.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recommended mitigation for ownership skew before a large reassignment?
options: Perform the entire reassignment as a single mass update during business hours
Switch the object's OWD to Private first
Reassign records in smaller batches (e.g., a couple thousand at a time), ideally off-peak
Disable the role hierarchy for the duration of the reassignment
questions.explain: Batching reassignments avoids forcing one enormous recalculation and spreads the load, typically scheduled outside business hours.

questions.q: What distinguishes lookup skew from account data skew?
options: Lookup skew only affects custom objects, account data skew only affects standard objects
Lookup skew involves records pointing at a shared target through a lookup field rather than many children sitting under one master-detail parent
Lookup skew is resolved by Restriction Rules, account data skew is not
There is no meaningful distinction between the two
questions.explain: Lookup skew is about many records referencing the same target via a plain lookup; account data skew specifically concerns a huge number of children under one parent Account, often via master-detail.
